elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2.2: "PB may terminate this Agreement for convenience at any time upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ". The original gating conditions ($60M Development Cost threshold; only prior to first Regulatory Approval) are deleted, so PB's election is unconditional. There are no Order Forms in this co-development structure, so Agreement-level coverage suffices. The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present" reported false, but that appears to be a literal-alias artefact (the customer is named "PB", not "Customer"); substantively the right is expressly granted.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ" replaces the redacted, undefined "[***]" notice period, fixing the blank trigger.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "and SFJ will refund pro rata any fees or other amounts prepaid by PB for the period after the effective date of termination" — the refund is expressly pro rata (not merely post-termination-period) and runs from Vendor (SFJ) to Customer (PB).

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Inserted sentence: "SFJ has no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the Term." "Term" is a defined concept (Section 14.1), so the anchor is not undefined. Retained SFJ exits (14.2.6 Change of Control, 14.2.10 JSC decision, and the other trigger-based rights) each require an external trigger and are therefore not at-will convenience rights that would contradict the new sentence.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Notice is set at thirty (30) days, outside the 60–90 day fallback band. This is deliberate (preferred level targeted) and is customer-favourable, but it does not satisfy the fallback element as written.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: The retained third sentence of 14.2.2 preserves the 300% of Development Costs buy-out payment on PB's termination, with no cap referenced to three months of fees. No fee cap of any kind is introduced.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Satisfied a fortiori: the inserted sentence bars SFJ from any convenience termination during the Term, which is more restrictive than confining it to term-end.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Conditional element; the condition does not apply because the redline removes any SFJ convenience termination right entirely, so no notice period for such a right is required.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements are met in operative language (unconditional PB convenience right, 30 days' written notice, express pro rata refund of prepayments, express bar on SFJ convenience termination during the Term). Nothing is left to the margin comment.

The deterministic 'Customer convenience termination present' flag (ok=false) is a false negative on substance: the clause names the customer as "PB" rather than a generic "Customer", and the operative grant "PB may terminate this Agreement for convenience at any time upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice" is plainly present.

Fallback is not met (30-day notice is outside the 60–90 day band and the retained 300% Development Cost buy-out is uncapped), but that is immaterial because the preferred checklist is complete; a level need only be satisfied at one tier.

Minimality holds: only the two gating conditions ($60M spend threshold and the pre-first-Regulatory-Approval window) and the blank [***] notice figure were removed — each removal is necessary to make the convenience right unconditional and the notice period certain — and the two insertions map one-to-one to the refund and no-Vendor-convenience elements. The 300% buy-out, Approval Payment carry-over, Section 6.2 adjustment and credit language are retained verbatim, and no survival tail, expense language or procedure was added.

Minor drafting note (not a minimality failure): the refund sentence reads "any fees or other amounts prepaid by PB" rather than "prepaid fees". The broadening is a reasonable adaptation because this agreement does not use "fees" as a defined payment concept (PB's payments are Approval Payments, Buy-Out Payment, etc.), so a fees-only refund would be inoperative here.

Intent is preserved: the retained buy-out economics, ARTICLE 6 cross-references, Section 11.1.1.4 Trial Data Package purchase mechanic and Section 6.2 adjustment all continue to function; the sentence "if PB elects to continue development ... following such termination" remains coherent now that termination may occur after first Regulatory Approval. No dangling cross-reference or undefined term is created.

Residual commercial exposure to flag to the client (correctly handled in the rationale rather than by a second redline): PB's exit still costs 300% of Development Costs plus continuing Approval Payments, so the exit is unconditional but not free; and SFJ's Section 14.2.10 JSC-disagreement right, while trigger-based, is close to discretionary in practice and may warrant separate negotiation if SFJ resists the new no-convenience sentence.
